## Catholic
Peter himself is the rock. Jesus gives Simon a new name and then builds on him, so the Church rests on Peter's person and office, which passes to the bishops of Rome who succeed him. The weight falls on the wordplay between Peter and rock, read as one and the same, and on the promise that Hades will not prevail. Paul writes, “I will give to you the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven,” and the keys go with the rock. It takes the words as Jesus' own words, spoken as the Gospel reports them, and the promise as a real act of Christ; it holds the Bible fully true and reads it with the Church's tradition. Held by the Catholic Church.

## Eastern Orthodox
The rock is Peter's confession in the verse before, and Peter as the one who confesses it. Many of the Fathers read it so, and Orthodox teaching holds that every bishop who keeps that confession sits in Peter's seat, so the verse founds the Church on right faith and on the whole episcopate. The weight falls on the confession and on the shift from Petros to petra. It takes the saying as Jesus' own words and the promise as real, holds the Bible fully true, and reads it with the Fathers. Held by the Orthodox Church.

## Reformed
The rock is Christ, confessed by Peter, who speaks for all the apostles; the Church is built on that confession, so no single office is founded here. The weight falls on the change of word from Petros to petra and on Scripture read with Scripture, where Christ is the one foundation (1 Corinthians 3:11) and the living stone (1 Peter 2:4–8). It takes the words as Jesus' own words and the promise as a real act of Christ; it holds the Bible fully true and the text alone as its authority. Held by Reformed and Presbyterian churches, and by most evangelical churches.

## Historical-critical
The saying is read as a later composition: Matthew's community reflecting on Peter's standing after his death, since Matthew alone uses the word assembly and alone records this promise. Some scholars defend it as an original saying, perhaps in Aramaic, where one word, Kepha, would stand for both name and rock. It treats the Gospel as a human record shaped by the community that kept it, and scholarly reconstruction as its authority. Held by critical scholars of several churches and of none, who are divided among themselves.

## Where they agree
All four read Peter as spokesman for the apostles' confession, the assembly as the one people Jesus gathers, and the gates of Hades as the power of death, which cannot destroy it.

## Where they part, and why
- Whether Petros and petra name the same thing: one rock for the Catholic reading, a shift that matters for the others.
- Whether what is founded is an office that passes on, a confession kept by all bishops, or the confession as such.
- Whether the words are Jesus' own or the community's: a question about the Gospel itself.
- What settles it: tradition, the Fathers, Scripture read with Scripture, or reconstruction.

## Where readings can be held together
Peter and his confession can both be foundational if Peter is understood as the confessing apostle. Peter and rock support that connection, while the confession itself appears in the surrounding verses; this requires reading the promise in its narrative context. The combination does not settle succession. A reading that affirms Jesus said these words conflicts with one that denies he did.

## What the text settles
The wordplay is in the text, and the confession stands in the verse before it, so a reading that separates the rock from the confession rests on little here. The Greek has two forms, Petros and petra, and the passage does not say whether the change is meant. Nothing in the verse speaks of succession, for or against.
